comment.value:
This paper introduces CLIMB, an automated framework designed to optimize the mixture of data used for pre-training Large Language Models (LLMs). Current pre-training often relies on manually curated datasets or raw web data without clear domain definitions, which limits the efficiency and performance of the resulting models. The CLIMB method proposes an automated framework that combines semantic clustering with an iterative search mechanism guided by proxy models and performance predictors.

**Main strengths**
- *Resources*: The authors release CLIMBLAB, a 1.2T-token dataset, to support further research, and CLIMBMIX for efficient pre-training.
- *Performance*: Models trained on CLIMBMIX (a 400B-token dataset discovered using CLIMB) outperformed existing data-mixing methods like DoReMi and Regmix. Specifically, a 1B-parameter model trained on CLIMBMIX surpassed the powerful Llama-3.2-1B by 2.0% on general reasoning tasks.
- *Efficiency*: The framework is compute-efficient, using proxy models and predictors to avoid the prohibitive cost of training full models on every potential mixture.

Following a successful rebuttal that addressed all concerns, the paper has achieved a strong consensus for acceptance, with four out of five reviewers recommending clear acceptance. This submission is well above the bar for the NeurIPS DB track and should be accepted.

Dear Reviewer jY8A,

Thank you for your thoughtful follow-up!

## Q1. “Optimizing diversity” claim

As shown in Figure 8 (iteration 3) of our paper, 17 out of 20 clusters receive non-zero weights, which ensures diversity. Even the clusters shown with a weight of 0.00 actually have small non-zero weights, but they are rounded due to precision limitations. For instance, cluster C14 has a weight of 0.004. Therefore, in practice, data from the majority of clusters is still sampled during training. We will clarify this point in the revised version.

## Q9. Random baseline

We acknowledge that our current wording may have caused confusion. Both our intended meaning and our actual implementation use the natural distribution as the random baseline. This is because the clusters vary significantly in size, and using uniform weights would lead to over-sampling from smaller clusters. We will revise the phrasing in the updated version to reflect this more clearly. Thank you for pointing it out!

We are really happy that our response has resolved Q2 and we sincerely appreciate your follow-up questions. They have been instrumental in helping us improve the clarity and quality of our work. Thanks!

## Q1. “Optimizing diversity” claim

> In CLIMB we measure diversity by **the effective number of clusters that receive non-zero weight**

and

> Consequently, the mixture is intentionally sparse

By your definition, wouldn't you then say that CLIMB produces non-diverse datasets, by being sparse (assigning a weight of zero to most clusters)?

## Q2. Human label v.s. Automatic label
Thank you for including this additional experiment, which I believe significantly strengthens the paper.

## Q9. Random baseline

> We used the original dataset distribution without applying any reweighting. 

In lines 572-573:

> Random: randomly select data for language model training, where each cluster is assigned **an equal and uniform weight**.

Can you clarify what "equal and uniform weight" means? If you assign an equal weight to each cluster, won't the amount of documents sampled from each cluster be the same, thus no longer using the natural distribution of the dataset (which most likely does not have the same number of documents per cluster)?

Dear Reviewer NB4Q,

We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful, constructive feedback and for highlighting the strengths of our work. Below we address each concern in turn, and we will incorporate the suggested clarifications and new results in our revised version.

## Q1. Scalability beyond 1B parameters
We strongly agree that demonstrating scalability is valuable. Since the initial submission we have run additional scaling-up experiments:
- Proxy model: Nemotron Transformer 1B
- Target model: Nemotron Transformer 8B

The results are shown as following:
| Method  | avg_math  | avg_code | avg_reasoning  | mmlu | mmlu_pro | AGIEval  | avg.  |
|------|--------|-------|--------|-------|--------|---------|--------|
 | Prev. SOTA  | 36.34 | 54.98   | 53.58 | 72.62 | 47.62 | 50.63  | 52.63 |
 | CLIMB  | 36.90 | 59.00   | 55.87 | 73.84 | 49.37 | 52.47  | 54.58 |

We can see that CLIMB yields an average of 1.85pp for 8B model, confirming that (a) the search space discovered by clustering remains meaningful at scale and (b) a smaller proxy model is sufficient to steer mixtures for much larger targets, preserving the computational advantage.
We will include these quantitative results and an expanded discussion of scaling experiments.

* Note: Since 8B model is more powerful and can do a lot more tasks, we included a new set of tasks for evaluation. Specifically, avg_math is an average of GSM8K and MATH500. Avg_code is an average of Humaneval, Humaneval+, MBPP, MBPP+. Avg_reasoning is an average of ARC_E, Race, PIQA, Winogrande, Hellaswag, ARC_C, OpenBookQA, SocialQA, CommonsenseQA.

## Q2. Evaluation on high-stakes domains

Thank you for your comment! Taking healthcare as an example, we have extended the evaluation to MedMCQA, a widely used and risk-sensitive medical benchmark. For this experiment, we directly used the CLIMB Mix optimized for MMLU-STEM, as described in Section 5 of our paper. This approach not only saves the time required for running CLIMB search on the new task, but also serves as a test of generalization, revealing how well CLIMB performs on unseen tasks. The results show that CLIMB Mix outperforms Random Mix by approximately about 3.7 percentage points. We will update the paper to include this result.
| Method  | avg_math  | 
|------|--------|
 | Random Mix  | 30.14 |
 | CLIMB Mix  | 33.82 |


We really appreciate your recognition of our contributions and the insightful suggestions. The new large-model experiments and high-stakes-domain evaluations corroborate CLIMB’s scalability and broad applicability. We believe these additions strengthen the paper and hope they could well address your concerns. Thank you again for your careful review and constructive comments!

Dear Reviewer Jjwc,

We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful evaluation and for recognizing the soundness, clarity, and practical relevance of our work. Below we address each concern point-by-point.
## Q1. Reasoning gains
As shown in Table 2 the experiments with longer training (400 B tokens), CLIMB’s 1 B model reaches 53.54 avg. on a 12-task reasoning suite (Table 2), surpassing Llama-3.2-1B by +2.0 pp, which was trained on 9 trillion tokens. This demonstrates significant improvement with our proposed approach.
Notably, CLIMB delivers substantial gains on the foremost reasoning-oriented benchmarks—including PIQA, ARC-C/E, HellaSwag, Winogrande, SIQA, MMLU, and OBQA.
## Q2. “Domain” definition
In Section 2.1 we create semantic domains automatically:
1. Embedding & k-means ($K_{init}$ = 1000) – yields fine-grained topical groups.
2. Cluster-level pruning – discard low-quality clusters using lightweight FastText quality classifiers.
3. Centroid merging – agglomerate similar clusters until Kenhanced = 21.


The resulting super-clusters act as proxy domains; no manual tags are required. We will add an explicit definition and illustrative examples (Appendix D.1) to strengthen the paper.
## Q3. Dataset and code release


We released our data at Huggingface and you can find it at `Dataset URL`.

Thanks for pointing it out! Yes, we are aware of this concern, and in our submission, we have accordingly designed two sets of experiments to address it. The first set involves mid-training on tasks that target general commonsense reasoning, ensuring that the model maintains strong generalization capabilities. The second set, based on MMLU, is intended to demonstrate the effectiveness of domain-specific optimization. While both are informative, we are more inclined toward the first setting, as it better preserves broad applicability. We will revise the paper to include a more detailed discussion and analysis of the trade-offs between these two approaches.

Thank you for your comment! We strongly agree that exploring more cost-effective strategies would make this work more promising and practical. To address this, we plan to explore more lightweight alternatives in future work.

Secondly, one can explore parameter-efficient scoring e.g., LoRA adapters so that each candidate can be evaluated by fine-tuning only <2 % of proxy weights.
Last but not least, we are inspired by recent studies that investigate the correlation between text compression efficiency and downstream performance (e.g., [1]). Such methods offer a promising direction for reducing the cost of data evaluation without requiring full model training, and we believe they could be integrated into our framework to improve scalability and accessibility.


[1] Predictive Data Selection: The Data That Predicts Is the Data That Teaches

Dear Reviewer jY8A,

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and constructive feedback.
Below we address every point raised and describe the concrete revisions we included into our paper.


## Q1. “Optimizing diversity” claim
Thank you for raising this point. In CLIMB we measure diversity by the effective number of clusters that receive non-zero weight. During the search procedure, the predictor assigns weight to clusters that are both (i) high quality for the target objective and (ii) complementary to one another. Consequently, the mixture is intentionally sparse yet far from monolithic: its dominant clusters cover distinct domains—for example, C6 (biology), C7 (chemistry), and C12 (mathematics)—which keeps the token distribution balanced across topics. As you noted, our primary focus is to optimize data quality, and we will revise the manuscript to clarify this definition of diversity and adjust our original claim accordingly. Thanks!


## Q2. Human label v.s. Automatic label


Thank you for highlighting the importance of an explicit ablation against manually curated domain labels. Because The Pile is now somewhat outdated and its quality has proven uneven, we re-ran the experiment on a newer, higher-quality internal corpus whose provenance we can disclose in aggregate.


- Experimental set-up




| Variant               | Label source                                                 | #Categories | CLIMB search applied? |
|-----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|-------------|------------------------|
| Human Labels + CLIMB search  | Data-source tags (Common-Crawl, Math, Code, SFT, Multilingual, Others) | 6           | ✓                      |
| Auto Clusters + CLIMB search | embedding + clustering (k = 6)            | 6           | ✓                      |




Both variants used identical model architecture (1 B parameters) and the same 12 downstream benchmarks.




- Results


On average, Auto Clusters + CLIMB search outperformed the Human Labels + CLIMB search by 1.5 percentage points across 12 tasks. The embedding-based clustering consistently surpassed the manually labeled counterpart, confirming that our fully automatic pipeline is at least as effective—and typically better—than human domain labeling while eliminating costly manual effort and subjective bias.


We will include the full ablation study in the revision and we hope this directly addresses the concern and strengthens the evidence for the effectiveness of our embedding + clustering approach.


## Q3. Broken data link & accessibility
We’re wrapping up our internal legal review and expect to release a raw-text version very soon. In addition, we will fix the broken link. Thanks!
## Q4. Typo and citation issues:


We will correct all noted typos and add missing citations for DCLM-baseline and all other datasets. We also referred to Figures 1&2 in our revised manuscript. Thanks!
## Q5. “throughout training” meaning
We iterate predictor training + sampling during search; once the best weights are chosen they stay fixed for full pre-training.  We will modify and state this explicitly.
## Q6. Model-based classifiers
Thanks for your question! These are the fasttext classifiers trained by ourselves as stated at lines 218-222.

## Q7. what data are proxy models pre-trained on?
The proxy models were pre-trained on the DCLM and TXT360 corpora. We will clarify this in the manuscript and add explicit citations to both datasets.
## Q8. Sampling inside a cluster / duplicates
A straightforward way to boost diversity inside each cluster is to bias sampling by a document’s distance from the cluster centroid. Because the centroid embedding is easy to compute, we can re-weight documents by a monotonic function of that distance—e.g., giving higher probability to items farther from the centroid—so that the sampler covers the long-tail of each cluster instead of repeatedly drawing the most “central” examples.
Whether duplicates appear depends on the total training budget N. If N \times w_k < T_k (where w_k is the mixture weight for cluster k and T_k is the token count of that cluster), the chance of sampling the same document twice is negligible. In all our experiments this inequality holds, so duplicates are effectively avoided.
We will include this discussion in the revised paper.

We used the original dataset distribution without applying any reweighting.

We combine Nemotron-CC and smollm-corpus, and then employ our proposed CLIMB-clustering to semantically reorganize and filter this data into 20 distinct clusters. Dear Reviewer axNp,

Thank you very much for your thoughtful review and insightful feedback! Below we address your main points individually:

## Q1. Robustness due to "black-box" models and approximations:

Thank you for your questions regarding the potential vulnerabilities introduced by relying on Nemotron-340B for initial cluster pruning and the predictor f(θ) for approximating the objective function. We designed CLIMB to be robust to these aspects, and we provide further clarification below.

### Regarding Nemotron-340B for initial clustering:

- Alternative annotator: We re-scored the same 1 million documents with llama-3.3-70b-instruct and retrained the fastText filters. Resulting clusters changed only ~4 % and the final 1B model’s average score dropped by only 0.04 pp.

- Prompt ablation: We wrote a totally different prompt template which increased low-quality clusters by 6 %, but the search quickly down-weighted them; final accuracy fell 0.03 pp.
These new experiments demonstrate that the iterative refinement is crucial for optimal performance, suggesting that the system is not overly sensitive to the model and prompt. 
We will add these experiments to §5 and discuss why the framework is agnostic to the exact quality signal.

### Regarding the predictor f(θ):
We sample mixture weights from a Dirichlet distribution, giving the regression model exposure to both sparse and dense extremes. In addition, we use predictor to prune less promising mixture weights during iteration. This choice lets us generate both highly sparse and nearly uniform allocations while keeping the expected mixture aligned with real data availability. 
Figure 9 already shows a 0.94 Spearman correlation on a held-out set sampled after the search finished.
To probe true extrapolation, we injected 20 previously unseen mixtures after iteration 3; correlation remained 0.92 and the best of those mixtures was still 0.18 pp below CLIMB’s chosen mixture.  We will report these numbers in Appendix D.10.

## Q2. CLIMB v.s. RegMix

Thanks for your question! We allocated identical compute budgets to RegMix and CLIMB in our experiments to ensure fairness. That is, CLIMB spreads its 112 proxy trainings over three iterations (64 + 32 + 16), whereas RegMix trains 112 proxy models directly in a single round. The iterative refinement therefore delivers CLIMB’s performance gains without any extra compute—just a smarter allocation of the same budget. We will add this clarification to the paper.

## Q3. Figure 5 suggests diminishing returns (e.g., STEM).
The curve of STEM with 1B model flattens because the optimum is reached quickly for those domains.  Nevertheless, iteration 3 still improves the 1B model on Social-Sciences by +1.61 pp over iteration 1 (40.18 -> 41.79).  Since later iterations cost only 25 % of the first (16 configs vs. 64), we retain them for robustness across domains.

## Q4. Proxy Model Size
Table 3 (Abl.proxy) shows a steady but modest improvement as the proxy model scales from 62 M → 132 M → 350 M—an overall gain of just +0.30 pp. In the revision we will emphasize that these diminishing returns must be weighed against the rising compute cost, and we will add a dedicated paragraph quantifying that trade-off.

## Q5. Choice of $K_{\text{init}}$
Thank you for your suggestion! We will add an additional analysis to reveal a clear “sweet spot’’ for the initial number of clusters:
- Too small ($K_{\text{init}}$ = 48, 64).

With only a few coarse clusters, documents on very different topics are mixed together.  The subsequent quality filter has difficulty separating good from bad data inside such heterogeneous buckets, so the remaining corpus is both noisy and less diverse, leading to a lower Avg score.

- Moderate ($K_{\text{init}}$ $\approx$ 100-1000).

Each cluster still contains a healthy number of tokens, but topic purity is greatly improved.  After we drop the obvious low-quality clusters, the surviving data are simultaneously clean (high purity) and varied (broad coverage), producing the best overall performance.

- Too large ($K_{\text{init}}$ = 1000-2000).

Token counts per cluster shrink sharply.  In the second-stage “21-way’’ re-clustering we must merge many tiny clusters, which often forces sub-optimal combinations and reduces Avg.  Moreover, CLIMB’s search procedure (sampling + proxy training + predictor) now explores a weight vector in a ~2000-dimensional simplex; the higher dimensionality increases noise and the risk of local optima.  Even though the final search space depends only on $K_{\text{enhanced}}$, an overly large $K_{\text{init}}$ tends to inflate $K_{\text{enhanced}}$ and degrades the precision of re-clustering, making the optimiser harder to converge.

We will add this discussion to the revision to clarify why moderate values of $K_{\text{init}}$ yield the strongest and most stable gains.  Thank you for highlighting the need for a more nuanced explanation.

Again, we appreciate the reviewer’s positive assessment and helpful suggestions, and we believe the above revisions will further strengthen the paper.

summary.value:
This paper addresses the critical challenge of optimizing data mixtures in large language model (LLM) pre-training. Instead of relying on manually curated datasets or raw web data with no clear domain delineation, the authors propose CLIMB—an automated framework that combines semantic clustering with an iterative search mechanism guided by proxy models and performance predictors. The method enables automatic discovery of latent data domains and learns optimal mixture weights in a compute-efficient manner.
Experiments demonstrate that a 1B-parameter model trained on CLIMBMIX (400B tokens), discovered via CLIMB, surpasses Llama-3.2-1B by 2.0% on general reasoning tasks. The authors further release two valuable resources: CLIMBLAB (1.2T tokens) for research purposes and CLIMBMIX for efficient pre-training.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The paper tackles a highly relevant and challenging problem at the heart of LLM development. The proposed CLIMB framework, which automates data mixture optimization through a "clustering + iterative search" paradigm, is a novel and valuable contribution that shifts the field from reliance on human heuristics to a more principled, data-driven approach.
- The experimental validation is convincing. CLIMB consistently outperforms strong baselines, including Random selection, DoReMi, and RegMix, across multiple model scales (Table 1). Crucially, the resulting 950M model demonstrates state-of-the-art performance, surpassing established models like Llama-3.2-1B on a suite of reasoning benchmarks (Table 2). This provides clear evidence of the method's efficacy.
- Beyond the framework itself, the public release of the meticulously curated 1.2T-token CLIMBLAB corpus and the optimized 400B-token CLIMBMIX dataset is a major contribution. This greatly facilitates future research and reproducibility in this domain and stands as a key highlight of the submission.
- The paper is supported by a comprehensive set of experiments, including not only comparisons with SOTA models but also targeted optimizations for specific domains (Figure 5) and extensive ablation studies on key components of the framework (Table 3). This makes the conclusions highly robust.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Major Weaknesses:

1.  The framework’s robustness is potentially undermined by its reliance on a cascade of "black-box" models and approximations. While the end-to-end results are strong, the paper could benefit from a deeper discussion of the error propagation and sensitivity at each stage.
    1) Sec 3.1, lines 218-223:** The foundation of the entire method—the initial data clustering—rests on annotations from Nemotron-340B for subjective qualities like "educational value." This makes the framework's output sensitive to the specific capabilities and biases of this external model and the chosen prompt design (Appendix D.11). It would be valuable to understand how substituting this model or altering the prompts might change the resulting data clusters and, consequently, the final performance.
    2) Sec 2.2, Eq. 1 & 2: The use of a predictor `f(θ)` to approximate the true objective function introduces a potential vulnerability. While the high Spearman correlation (Fig. 9) is encouraging, it is validated on a subset of configurations already deemed promising by the search. Its accuracy in the vast, unexplored regions of the configuration space is unknown. There is a risk that an imperfect predictor could prematurely guide the iterative search into a local optimum, preventing the discovery of a globally superior data mixture.

2.  The paper could do more to justify the considerable complexity of the framework against the achieved performance gains. The multi-stage process is resource-intensive, and it's not entirely clear if the added complexity consistently pays off.
    1) Table 1: When compared to RegMix—which is effectively a single-shot version of CLIMB—the 1B model shows a performance lift of about one percentage point (60.41% vs. 59.37%). While positive, this raises questions about the cost-benefit trade-off. Is the significant overhead of multiple iterations justified for this level of improvement across all use cases?
    2) Figure 5: The iterative nature of the search appears to offer limited benefits in some domain-specific optimizations. For example, in the MMLU-STEM task for the 1B model, the performance curves plateau almost immediately after the first iteration. This suggests that for certain tasks, the iterative refinement is not as impactful, and a simpler, single-round search might have yielded comparable results with far less compute. This phenomenon warrants further analysis.

Minor Weaknesses:

1. The claim that using the "largest feasible proxy model" is consistently best (line 652) is hard to reconcile with the data. While the 350M proxy yields a small 0.3% gain over the 62M proxy (Table 3), the results in Appendix D.9 (Table 6) show that the 62M proxy still enables the final 1B model to reach a strong performance of 60.11%. The paper would be more balanced if it discussed the clear trade-off between the marginal performance gain and the significant increase in computational cost for the proxy model.

2.  The explanation for why performance drops when `K_init` increases to 2000—that the clustering becomes "overly fine-grained"—is too general. A more nuanced analysis is needed to distinguish between two possibilities: (1) the search space simply becomes too large for the optimizer to handle effectively, or (2) the fine-grained clusters themselves are inherently of lower quality or less meaningful.

The embedding+clustering method is introduced as an alternative to human curated domain labels, but a comparison on a dataset containing them, such as The Pile, is lacking. Showing that CLIMB (with the proposed embedding+clustering approach) outperforms the search part of CLIMB applied on the original The Pile labels would make a strong case for the proposed embedding+clustering approach. Some additional notes/comments/questions:
- Some datasets in Figure 1 are missing citations
- “pertaining” -> “pre-training” (line 30)
- Figures 2 and 3 seem to not be referenced from the main text
- “throughout training” is mentioned several times (e.g., lines 72, 105). What does this mean exactly? Aren’t the final mixing weights defined before training of a model (as the one trained on ClimbMix) starts?
- “data” -> “dataset” (108)
- line 134: which model-based classifiers? The ones used in Nemotron-cc?
- line 202: what data are these models pre-trained on?
- line 255: “method” -> “model”

The paper is well organized and extremely detailed. summary.value: This paper introduces CLIMB, a novel and automated framework to optimize the data mixture for pre-training large language models. The core idea is to first use embedding and clustering to automatically group large-scale, unlabeled data into semantic domains. Then, it uses an iterative search process, powered by smaller proxy models and a predictor, to efficiently find the optimal mixing weights for these domains. The goal is to maximize model performance on target tasks without relying on expensive manual data curation.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The proposed CLIMB framework is a well-designed and effective solution to the challenging problem of data mixture optimization. Its ability to automatically discover domains from unlabeled text and iteratively refine the data recipe is a significant contribution that reduces the reliance on manual heuristics and pre-existing labels.

- The paper's investigation into optimizing pre-training data for specific domains (e.g., Social Sciences, STEM) is particularly valuable and has strong practical utility. The experiments clearly demonstrate that this targeted approach can lead to significant performance improvements in specialist models, which is a very useful finding for the community.




- The empirical results are strong and convincing. The method consistently outperforms well-established baselines like DoReMi and RegMix across various model sizes. The fact that the resulting 1B model surpasses a strong model like Llama-3.2-1B under the same token budget is impressive. The release of the CLIMBLAB and CLIMBMIX datasets is also a welcome contribution to the research community.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The paper does not directly evaluate the full fine-tuning downstream adaptability of a domain-specialized model. For instance, the authors show that a model pre-trained with a CLIMB-optimized social-science mix performs better in few-shot evaluations. However, the paper is missing a direct comparison between the following two scenarios: (A) a model pre-trained with the CLIMB social-science mix and then fully fine-tuned on social-science data, versus (B) a generally pre-trained model that is fine-tuned on the exact same social-science data. Such an experiment would provide a more complete understanding of how a specialized pre-training phase benefits the final, fine-tuned model's performance.


- While the optimized models show good generalization, there is a potential risk that over-optimizing for a very narrow domain could lead to a loss of capability in other areas. The paper acknowledges this possibility, stating that data mixture optimization "may lead to an overrepresentation of certain domains while underrepresenting others, potentially reinforcing knowledge disparities". A more in-depth analysis of these trade-offs would strengthen the work.

- The iterative search process, while more efficient than brute-force methods, still requires considerable computational resources to train multiple proxy models. As noted in the limitations, "training these proxy models still incurs non-negligible costs". Further exploration of more cost-effective evaluation strategies could enhance the framework's accessibility.

summary.value: Contemporary pre-training corpora often lack explicit domain segmentation, which limits the ability of language models to adapt efficiently to specialized domains. This paper proposes CLIMB, an automated framework for optimizing pre-training data mixtures. The approach embeds large-scale textual data into a semantic space and performs clustering to identify coherent data partitions. It then leverages small-scale proxy models and a learned utility predictor to iteratively search for and refine high-quality data mixtures. By doing so, CLIMB enables effective domain adaptation without relying on manually curated datasets, offering a scalable and principled alternative to traditional pre-training paradigms.

strengths_contributions.value:
1.Proposes an embedding-based data mixture approach that automatically identifies, groups, and combines high-quality clustered data for domain-specific pre-training, eliminating the reliance on manually defined domain partitions.

2.Introduces an iterative search procedure that dynamically refines data mixtures during training, improving both diversity and domain relevance while addressing scalability challenges in clustering and data filtering at trillion-token scale.

3.Constructs a filtered corpus of 1.2 trillion tokens across 20 semantically coherent clusters as a new platform for data-centric pre-training research, and releases a 400-billion-token high-quality dataset optimized for efficient large-scale language model training.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1.While the paper demonstrates performance improvements on a 1B-parameter model (as shown in the experimental section), it lacks a systematic discussion on the scalability of the proposed method to larger models (e.g., 7B or 13B). title.value: Nemotron-CLIMB: Clustering-based Iterative Data Mixture Bootstrapping for Language Model Pre-training

TLDR.value: Nemotron-CLIMB automates data mixture optimization for pre-training, improving domain adaptation and outperforming Llama-3.2-1B by 2.0% on general reasoning.

abstract.value:
Pre-training datasets are typically collected from web content and lack inherent domain divisions. For instance, widely used datasets like Common Crawl do not include explicit domain labels, while manually curating labeled datasets such as The Pile is labor-intensive. Consequently, identifying an optimal pre-training data mixture remains a challenging problem, despite its significant benefits for pre-
training performance. To address these challenges, we propose CLustering-based Iterative Data Mixture Bootstrapping (Nemotron-CLIMB), an automated framework that discovers, evaluates, and refines data mixtures in a pre-training setting. Specifically, Nemotron-CLIMB embeds and clusters large-scale datasets in a semantic space and then iteratively searches for optimal mixtures using a smaller proxy model and a predictor. This strategy enables effective domain adaptation without relying solely on curated data. When continuously trained on 400B tokens with this mixture, our 1B model exceeds the state-of-the-art Llama-3.2-1B by 2.0%. Moreover, we observe that optimizing for a specific domain (e.g., Social Sciences) yields a 5% improvement over random sampling. Finally, we introduce Nemotron-ClimbLab, a filtered 1.2-trillion-token corpus with 20 clusters as a research playground, and Nemotron-ClimbMix, a compact yet powerful 400-billion-token dataset designed for efficient pre-training that delivers superior performance under an equal token budget. We analyze the final data mixture, elucidating the characteristics of an optimal data mixture.

code_URL.description: If your submission includes code, provide the URL to a hosting platform (e.g., Github, Bitbucket) as described in the CFPs. See the main track [code guidelines](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for details.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
